title: Display and Visibility
summary: The CSS display property helps decide how a page part takes up space.
introduction: The CSS display property helps decide how a page part takes up space. Some parts start a new line. Others sit beside words. Compare these choices before moving on to rows and grids.
learningObjectives: Describe the behaviour of block, inline and inline-block boxes
Hide elements with display: none, visibility: hidden or a visually-hidden class, choosing the right one for accessibility
Use display: flow-root and display: contents appropriately

blocks.text: Every element has a default `display` value. **Block** elements (`div`, `p`, headings, `ul`, `li`, `section`) start on a new line and stretch across the full width of their container; `width`, `height` and all margins apply to them. **Inline** elements (`a`, `span`, `strong`, `em`, `code`) flow along the line of text and are sized by their content: `width` and `height` are ignored, vertical margins are ignored, and vertical padding is painted but does not push neighbouring lines apart. Images are a special *inline replaced* case: they sit in the line but accept `width` and `height`.

blocks.text: The first span keeps the size of its text and the 30px margin does nothing. The second, as an `inline-block`, becomes a 200 by 40 pixel box with a top margin, while still sitting in the line.

You can give any element any display value. Turning list items into `inline-block` boxes puts them on one line, which was the classic way to build a horizontal menu. The gap between them is the whitespace between the `li` tags in the HTML, rendered as a space, which is one reason flexbox replaced this technique for layout; it remains useful for badges and buttons that must flow with text.
Hiding things: none, hidden and visually hidden

`display: none` removes the element from layout entirely: it takes no space, cannot be focused and is removed from the accessibility tree, so screen readers do not announce it. `visibility: hidden` keeps the space the element occupied but makes it invisible and, likewise, hidden from assistive technology. `opacity: 0` only makes it transparent; it still takes space, can be tabbed to and is read aloud. For text that should be *only* for screen readers (the label of an icon button, a "skip to content" link until it is focused) the convention is a visually-hidden class that shrinks the element to a 1px clipped box without hiding it from anyone who cannot see the screen.

blocks.title: The visually-hidden utility
display: none hides from everyone
blocks.text: Hiding a text label with `display: none` so that only an icon shows also hides it from screen reader users, who are then left with an unlabelled button. Use the `.visually-hidden` class for text that must remain available to assistive technology, and reserve `display: none` for content that nobody should get, such as a closed menu.

`display: flex` and `display: grid` keep the element as a block box on the outside but change how its *children* are laid out; the next lessons are about them. `inline-flex` and `inline-grid` do the same for a container that must sit in a line of text. `display: flow-root` creates a new *block formatting context*: it contains floated children and stops a child's margin from collapsing through the parent, which is the clean fix for the leaking-margin problem from the box model lesson. `display: contents` makes the element's own box disappear so that its children behave as children of its parent; it is handy for a wrapper that gets in the way of a flex or grid layout, but avoid it on buttons, tables and lists, where some browsers have dropped the element's semantics along with its box.

blocks.title: Two-value display
blocks.text: Modern browsers also accept the two-value syntax `display: block flex;` or `display: inline grid;`, which names the outer box type and the inner layout separately. The single keywords are shorthands for these pairs; you will mostly keep writing `flex` and `grid`, but the two-value form explains what they mean.

questions.question: Which declaration hides an element but keeps the space it occupied on the page?
questions.explanation: `visibility: hidden` leaves the box in the layout but does not paint it. `display: none` removes the box and its space.

questions.question: `width: 300px` on a `span` with its default display makes it 300px wide.
questions.explanation: A span is inline, and inline boxes ignore `width` and `height`. Change its display to `inline-block` or `block` first.
